issues.explanation: 'Heavy make-up' is hard to reconcile with this patient's demographics (22-year-old single male auditor) and the rest of the profile unless there is a specific unreported context such as concealment or gender expression. In this profile it stands out as clinically implausible relative to the other items, whereas the other maladaptive strategies center on vigilance, escape, and social evaluation.

vignette:
Omar is a 22-year-old auditor who had been in his first serious relationship when he was raped by his ex-boyfriend after an evening at the other man’s apartment. He remembers the scene in concrete sensory fragments: the heavy scent of his ex’s cologne mixed with sweat, the abrupt movement when his ex blocked the doorway, the shock of hearing familiar words spoken in a tone that made refusal feel pointless. What continues to disturb Omar is not only the assault itself but the sense that something deeply wrong and degrading was done to him by someone he had trusted. Since then, phrases that sound like the way his ex used to speak to him can make his stomach drop, and when he encounters a similar smell on a crowded elevator or in the hallway outside a client meeting, he feels thrown back into that night and flooded with humiliation.

In the weeks afterward, Omar became preoccupied with what the assault said about him. He had come to believe that somebody stronger, smarter, or less naive would not have gotten into that situation. He compares himself constantly to an imagined other man who would have seen the danger sooner, left earlier, fought harder. Alongside that self-comparison is a more global loss: he describes himself as having once been easygoing and upbeat, and now feeling persistently miserable, as if that version of himself has been replaced by someone smaller and ashamed. Encounters that remind him of his ex, or even seeing people behave in ways he experiences as selfish, boundary-violating, or morally wrong, do not simply upset him; they revive the conviction that he has been permanently humiliated.

That belief has shaped how he moves through the world. At work, where he spends long hours in conference rooms with clients and senior staff reviewing financial discrepancies, he is acutely aware of being observed. He avoids situations in which his appearance or performance might be scrutinized more than necessary, speaking less in meetings when he can, dreading presentations, and choosing loose, concealing clothing that makes him feel less exposed. He often seats himself near the door in audit meetings or training sessions so he can leave quickly if he starts to feel trapped. The logic makes immediate sense to him: if being noticed is dangerous and if he has already shown himself to be the kind of person to end up degraded, then minimizing visibility feels like the only way to protect himself.

Over time his body has come to operate as if danger is always close. Omar describes himself as constantly tense, with his shoulders tight and his attention scanning the room before he can settle. Sudden movements from other people—someone reaching across a table too quickly, a coworker stepping behind him unexpectedly—put him instantly on guard. Because unfamiliar places feel impossible to assess, he avoids them whenever he can, preferring known routes, known coffee shops, known office spaces. That persistent sense of threat feeds directly into his habits of protection: he checks where the exits are almost automatically, declines invitations to new venues after work, and chooses seats that keep other people in view.

The habits that were meant to make him safer have narrowed his life and seem to keep the problem alive. By sticking to the edges of rooms and dressing to disappear, he remains intensely focused on whether anyone is noticing him, whether someone is moving too close, whether a smell in the air resembles his ex’s cologne. The more he scans, the more readily those reminders seem to appear. A client’s aftershave, a stranger’s sudden gesture, or a joking phrase that echoes his ex can set off the same jolt. When that happens and he slips out early or avoids the next situation entirely, he is left feeling even more different from other people and more convinced that the assault has marked him in a lasting way. In his mind, the precautions also become evidence: if he has to live like this, he tells himself, then maybe he really is damaged and permanently diminished.

This has begun to affect his work and his relationships. He remains competent as an auditor, but he has started turning down opportunities that would place him in unfamiliar offices or require more visible performance. He stays single and keeps interactions carefully bounded. What finally brought him to treatment was the realization that his world had become organized around escape routes, vigilance, and avoidance, and that even routine workdays could be derailed by a smell in an elevator or a comment that sounded too much like his ex. What frightens Omar most is that he may never stop feeling humiliated and on guard. What he hopes, more quietly, is that he might recover some sense of safety without having to disappear.
